summary: This paper develops a unified description of strong-drive limits in flux- and charge-driven Josephson circuits across drive frequency and dc flux bias using classical phase-space analysis and Floquet–Markov simulations. At low frequency, bound-state resonances and separatrix chaos govern the response with a dc-bias-dependent chaos threshold, while at high frequency a distinct unbound-resonance transition occurs where the dissipative steady state transfers from the central bound-state region to outer resonances formed by above-barrier running trajectories.
motivation: Strong microwave drives enable fast measurement and parametric control in superconducting circuits but induce transitions out of the intended low-energy manifold at large amplitudes. Understanding these intrinsic strong-drive limitations across different drive channels and frequencies is essential for extending reliable operation in driven Josephson devices.
method: The authors perform Floquet–Markov simulations of driven SQUID systems including dissipation, supplemented by classical Poincaré analysis and analytical criteria derived from Melnikov theory and Bessel-function arguments. They validate the low-frequency dc-flux-bias dependence experimentally in a flux-driven SQUID and verify parametric exchange rates above the unbound-resonance threshold through coherent simulations.
result: At low frequency, the chaos threshold follows $\max\{|M_1|, |M_2|\} = 1$ with $M_1, M_2$ from Melnikov analysis, strongly dependent on $\phi_{\text{dc}}$. At high frequency, the unbound-resonance threshold is determined by $J_0(\phi_{\text{ac}}^*) = J_2(\phi_{\text{ac}}^*)$ giving $\phi_{\text{ac}}^* = 0.59\pi$ (independent of drive frequency and nearly independent of circuit parameters), controlling the onset of steady-state transfer to outer resonances. Parametric operation persists beyond this threshold but at reduced rates, setting an effective speed limit. Experimental verification of the low-frequency $\phi_{\text{dc}}$ dependence in a SQUID with $E_C/2\pi = 0.09$ GHz, $E_J/2\pi = 66$ GHz, and $g/2\pi = 39$ MHz confirms the predictions.
